title: Torsional selection rule for the spin--orbit conversion of light
abstract: Standard Pancharatnam-Berry and linear-birefringent media convert optical spin into orbital angular momentum (OAM) through an anisotropy \emph{director}, a rank-two, headless field, and therefore obey the selection rule $Δ\ell=2q$ per unit texture charge $q$. We show that a medium with geometric \emph{torsion}, the continuum limit of a screw-dislocation array, can convert spin to OAM through the \emph{contortion} of its material connection, which enters the effective paraxial dynamics as a rank-one vector field. The resulting selection rule is $Δ\ell=q$. Its winding is fixed by geometry and symmetry, not by a Pancharatnam--Berry director, and the process conserves the screw charge $\tilde J_z=L_z+(q/2)σ_z$ while exchanging $(2-q)\hbar$ of angular momentum per converted photon with the defect lattice. Paraxial simulations confirm the rule: a circular Gaussian input develops a stable, topologically quantized $\ell=+q$ vortex in the reversed helicity, with $83\%$ conversion over three Rayleigh ranges and no fine-tuning. We propose a polarization-resolved photonic-lattice discriminator in which the slope of the measured OAM versus the independently written texture charge, one for torsion, two for birefringence, separates the two mechanisms.
summary: This paper introduces a novel mechanism where light's spin can convert into orbital angular momentum (OAM) via material torsion, yielding the selection rule $\Delta\ell=q$. This contrasts sharply with the standard Pancharatnam–Berry effect ($\Delta\ell=2q$). The authors confirm this theoretically and propose an experiment using patterned photonic lattices to measure this distinct signature.
main_problem: The paper aims to distinguish between two mechanisms for converting light's spin angular momentum (SAM) into orbital angular momentum (OAM): the standard Pancharatnam–Berry (PB) mechanism and a novel process mediated by geometric torsion.
main_result: Torsion predicts a selection rule $\Delta\ell=q$, which is distinct from the PB prediction of $\Delta\ell=2q$. This difference can be experimentally verified using polarization-resolved photonic lattice discriminators.
method: The authors use paraxial simulations to confirm the theoretical selection rules and propose an experimental setup involving femtosecond-written photonic lattices for measurement.
model_or_system: The system involves light propagating through a medium exhibiting geometric torsion, modeled using Riemann–Cartan geometry. The dynamics are governed by an effective paraxial Maxwell model coupling circular polarization to spatial structure via contortion and torsional phase rates.
key_observables: The ratio of measured OAM ($\ell$) versus the independently written texture charge ($q$); sideband positions showing slopes of 1 (torsion) vs. 2 (PB).
important_parameters: Texture charge $q$, conversion efficiency $\eta \approx 83\%$, and the topological quantization of the resulting vortex ($\ell=+q$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes the coupling is linear in the written contortion vector for the proposed experiment, and it contrasts the torsion mechanism with the standard PB director formalism.
figures_summary: Figure 3 predicts that OAM vs. texture charge plots will show non-overlapping sidebands: $\Delta\ell=q$ for torsion and $\Delta\ell=2q$ for PB coupling.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical difference in selection rules ($\Delta\ell=2q$ vs. $\Delta\ell=q$) based on the underlying geometry (director vs. contortion). It then presents paraxial simulations confirming the torsional rule and concludes by proposing a concrete, polarization-resolved discriminator experiment.
why_interesting: This work provides a clean, geometrically derived physical mechanism for light-matter interaction that deviates from standard optical models, offering a new platform to probe fundamental concepts like geometric torsion in photonics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The selection rule distinguishes the rank of the me- diating field. (a) A Pancharatnam–Berry element couples the circular components through a rank-two director texture of charge q; the coupling winds as e±i2qφ. (b) A torsional (Riemann–Cartan) medium couples them through the rank- one contortion vector, which winds as e±iqφ. (c),(d) Simu- lated OAM spectra of the converted beam E−for the same texture charge q = 1 and identical coupling magnitude: the sideband appears at ℓ= +2 (PB) versus ℓ= +1 (torsional).

FIG. 2. Torsional vortex generation (q = 1). (a) Phase of the converted field at z = 25 w0: a stable, charge-n=+1 spiral. (b) Conversion η = P−and mean OAM versus propagation distance; both saturate at 0.83. (c) Final conversion versus holonomy strength κ0: a broad maximum (η ≃0.85) with no fine-tuning; in every run the charge is quantized at n = +1. Full sweeps in (κ0, Γ0), paraxial parameter k0 = 8–64, and grid refinement are given in the SM [27].
